title: Geometry
tagline: From points and lines to measuring the world.

nodes.label: Point
nodes.defines: the floor for location — an undefined notion; everything else is built from collections of points
nodes.summary: An exact location with no size.

nodes.label: Line
nodes.defines: the floor for straightness — an undefined notion of infinite extent with no width
nodes.summary: Perfectly straight, endless both ways, with no width.

nodes.label: Plane
nodes.defines: the floor for flatness — an undefined notion of two-dimensional extent; the ambient space everything else lives in
nodes.summary: A perfectly flat surface that goes on forever.

nodes.label: Distance
nodes.defines: first radical — the metric; assigns a non-negative number to every pair of points
nodes.summary: How far apart two points are — never negative, the same both ways.

nodes.label: Angle
nodes.defines: second radical — rotation; assigns a measure to the turning between two rays sharing a vertex; not reducible to distance
nodes.summary: The amount of turn between two paths that start at the same point.

nodes.label: Line segment
nodes.defines: bounded portion of a line between two endpoints; its length is the distance between them
nodes.summary: The straight piece of a line between two endpoints; its length is the distance between them.

nodes.label: Ray
nodes.defines: half-line: an endpoint together with all points of a line on one side of it
nodes.summary: A straight path that starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction.

nodes.label: Measuring angles
nodes.defines: the numeric value of an angle (degrees); classified acute / right / obtuse / straight / reflex
nodes.summary: How big a turn is, in degrees — acute, right, obtuse or straight.

nodes.label: Parallel lines
nodes.defines: coplanar lines that never meet; a transversal makes corresponding and alternate-interior angles equal
nodes.summary: Lines that never meet; a line crossing them makes matching equal angles.

nodes.label: Polygons
nodes.defines: closed plane figure bounded by line segments — has vertices, sides, and interior angles
nodes.summary: A closed flat shape with straight sides; its inside angles add to (n − 2) × 180°.

nodes.label: Slides, turns and flips
nodes.defines: a transformation of the plane (translation, rotation, reflection) that preserves both distance and angle measure — the floor for 'sameness of shape'
nodes.summary: Sliding, turning or flipping a shape without changing its size or shape.

nodes.label: Triangles
nodes.defines: three-sided polygon; interior angles always sum to 180°
nodes.summary: A three-sided shape whose angles always add up to 180°.

nodes.label: Congruent shapes
nodes.defines: two figures related by a rigid motion — 'same size and same shape', written ≅
nodes.summary: Exactly the same size and shape — one fits on the other after a slide, turn or flip.

nodes.label: Circles
nodes.defines: set of all points at a fixed distance (the radius) from a center point
nodes.summary: Every point the same distance (the radius) from a centre.

nodes.label: Proving triangles match
nodes.defines: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS — minimal sets of equal measurements that force two triangles to be congruent
nodes.summary: SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS — three matching parts that prove two triangles are identical.

nodes.label: Similar shapes
nodes.defines: rigid motion composed with a uniform scaling (dilation) — preserves angle measure and ratios of distances; 'same shape, possibly different size', written ∼
nodes.summary: Same shape, different size: equal angles and sides in the same ratio.

nodes.label: Four-sided shapes
nodes.defines: four-sided polygon — parallelograms, trapezoids, rectangles, rhombi, squares, classified by which sides/angles are equal or parallel
nodes.summary: A four-sided shape — parallelograms, rectangles, rhombi, squares and more; angles add to 360°.

nodes.label: The coordinate plane
nodes.defines: Cartesian (x, y) representation of the plane — every point becomes an ordered pair of numbers
nodes.summary: A grid where every point is a pair of numbers (x, y).

nodes.label: Spotting similar triangles
nodes.defines: AA, SAS∼, SSS∼ — minimal sets of equal angles or proportional sides that force two triangles to be similar
nodes.summary: AA, SAS∼ and SSS∼ — quick tests that two triangles are similar.

nodes.label: Area
nodes.defines: measure of the two-dimensional region enclosed by a polygon or circle
nodes.summary: How much flat space a shape covers, in square units.

nodes.label: Pythagoras' theorem
nodes.defines: in a right triangle, a² + b² = c² — the metric radical (side lengths) meets the rotational radical (the right angle) for the first time
nodes.summary: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c² — the two short sides' squares add up to the longest side's square.

nodes.label: Angles in circles
nodes.defines: inscribed angle, central angle, tangent–chord, and arc–chord relationships — angle measure governs the geometry of circles
nodes.summary: Angle rules in circles: an angle at the edge is half the angle at the centre on the same arc.

nodes.label: The distance formula
nodes.defines: d = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²) — the Pythagorean theorem restated in coordinates
nodes.summary: Pythagoras on a grid: the straight-line distance between two points.

nodes.label: Sin, cos and tan
nodes.defines: sin, cos, tan — ratios of side lengths (distance) determined entirely by an acute angle (angle) in a right triangle; the ratio is invariant under similarity — both radicals meet here
nodes.summary: sin, cos and tan — side ratios in a right triangle that depend only on the angle.

applications.label: Navigation & surveying
applications.defines: GPS trilateration and surveying triangulation both reduce to solving triangles with trigonometric ratios and the distance formula

applications.label: Architecture & building
applications.defines: squaring foundations (3-4-5 triangles), computing material quantities (area), and scaling blueprints (similarity)

applications.label: Computer graphics & games
applications.defines: every on-screen animation is a composition of rigid motions and similarity transformations on coordinate data

applications.label: Astronomy
applications.defines: measuring distances to celestial objects via parallax and triangulation — trigonometric ratios applied at planetary scale

applications.label: Art & design
applications.defines: tessellation, perspective drawing, and logo scaling are rigid motions and similarity transformations made visible

summaries.point: An exact location with no size.
summaries.line: Perfectly straight, endless both ways, with no width.
summaries.plane: A perfectly flat surface that goes on forever.
summaries.distance: How far apart two points are — never negative, the same both ways.
summaries.angle: The amount of turn between two paths that start at the same point.

cards.text: Every shape you've ever drawn — a house, a star, a pizza slice — is made from just **five ideas**. Can you guess one of them?
cards.reveal: The five are **point, line, plane, distance** and **angle**. Geometry doesn't define them; it builds everything else out of them.

cards.text:
**Point** — an exact location. It has no size at all, just a position.

**Line** — perfectly straight, endless in both directions, with no width.

**Plane** — a perfectly flat surface that goes on forever, like an endless sheet of paper.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 120"><polygon class="soft" points="20,95 70,25 230,25 180,95"/><line class="a" x1="40" y1="80" x2="200" y2="40"/><circle class="dot" cx="120" cy="60" r="4"/><text x="126" y="76">point</text><text x="196" y="34">line</text><text x="26" y="112">plane</text></svg>

cards.q: Which one has a position but **no size** at all?

options.why: Right — a point only marks where something is. The dot you draw is just a picture of it.

options.feedback: A line has length (endless, in fact). A point has no length, width or area.
A plane stretches out in two directions. A point is the one with no size.

cards.text:
**Distance** — how far apart two points are. It's always zero or positive, and A to B is the same as B to A.

**Angle** — the amount of turn between two straight paths that start at the same point.

cards.q: You walk from your door to the shop, then back. Is the distance back longer, shorter or the same?
cards.reveal: The same. Distance doesn't care about direction — A to B equals B to A.

cards.q: Two roads leave a crossroads. The amount you'd turn to go from one road onto the other is…

options.why: Yes — an angle measures turn between two paths from one point.

options.feedback: Distance is how far apart two points are. Turning is measured by an angle.
A plane is a flat surface. The turn between two roads is an angle.

review.q: Which of the five building blocks measures **how far apart** two points are?

options.feedback: An angle measures turn, not separation.
A line is a straight path; the separation of two points is their distance.

angle_measure.title: Measuring angles
angle_measure.summary: How big a turn is, in degrees — acute, right, obtuse or straight.

cards.text: Skateboarders talk about a "180" and a "360". What are they counting?
cards.reveal: **Degrees** of turn. A 360 is one full spin; a 180 is half a spin.

cards.text:
We measure angles in **degrees (°)**. A full turn is 360°.

- **Acute**: less than 90°
- **Right**: exactly 90° (a square corner)
- **Obtuse**: between 90° and 180°
- **Straight**: exactly 180° (a straight line)

cards.q: An angle measures 135°. What kind is it?

options.why: 135° is more than 90° but less than 180°.

options.feedback: Acute angles are smaller than 90°. 135° is bigger.
Straight is exactly 180°. 135° is less than that.

cards.title: Angles that add up
cards.problem: Two angles that make a right angle together are **complementary** (sum 90°). Two that make a straight line are **supplementary** (sum 180°). What's the supplement of 110°?
steps: Supplementary means the two add to 180°.

cards.q: What is the **complement** of 35°?
A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices from the centre. What angle is each slice?

review.q: What is the supplement of 65°?
A square corner measures…

options.feedback: 180° is a straight line. A square corner is a right angle, 90°.
45° is half a right angle. A square corner is 90°.

area.title: Area
area.summary: How much flat space a shape covers, in square units.

cards.text: You're tiling a floor 7 m long and 4 m wide with 1 m square tiles. How many tiles do you need — without counting?
cards.reveal: **28** — that's the floor's **area**, 7 × 4 square metres.

cards.text:
**Area** is how much flat space a shape covers, in **square units** (cm², m²).

- Rectangle: **length × width**
- Parallelogram: **base × height**
- Triangle: **½ × base × height**

The height is always measured **at right angles** to the base.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 90"><polygon points="20,80 140,80 100,20"/><line class="a" x1="100" y1="20" x2="100" y2="80"/><rect class="a" x="100" y="72" width="8" height="8"/><text x="104" y="50">h</text><text x="70" y="94">base</text><text x="150" y="50">½ × b × h</text></svg>

cards.title: Why a triangle is half
cards.problem: Why does a triangle get ½ × base × height?
steps: Make a copy of the triangle and turn it around.
The two fit together into a **parallelogram** with the same base and height.
So one triangle is **half** of base × height.

cards.q: A triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 cm. What is its area?
A parallelogram has base 9 m and height 5 m. What is its area?

review.q: A rectangle is 12 cm by 5 cm. What is its area?
The height of a triangle must be measured…

options.text: At right angles to the base

options.feedback: A slanted side is usually longer than the height. Height is perpendicular to the base.

options.text: From the middle of the base to anywhere
options.feedback: Height is the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite corner.

circle.title: Circles
circle.summary: Every point the same distance (the radius) from a centre.

cards.text: Tie a string to a peg, pull it tight and walk around. What shape do your footprints make — and why?
cards.reveal: A **circle** — every footprint is the same distance from the peg.

cards.text:
A **circle** is every point at the same distance from a **centre**.

- That distance is the **radius** (r).
- The **diameter** goes right across through the centre: d = 2r.
- The distance around is the **circumference**: C = 2πr (π ≈ 3.14).

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: A wheel has radius 3 cm. Find its diameter and circumference.

cards.q: A circle has radius 5 cm. What is its circumference? (Round to 2 decimal places.)
cards.hint: C = 2πr. Use π ≈ 3.1416 or your calculator's π.

cards.q: A circle's diameter is 14 cm. What is its radius?
cards.explain: The radius is half the diameter — 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm.

review.q: The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge is the…

options.feedback: The diameter goes all the way across — twice the radius.
The circumference is the distance around the circle.

circle_theorems.title: Angles in circles
circle_theorems.summary: Angle rules in circles: an angle at the edge is half the angle at the centre on the same arc.

cards.text: Stand anywhere on the edge of a round fountain and look at the two ends of a diameter. What angle do your lines of sight make — wherever you stand?
cards.reveal: Always exactly **90°**. Circles hide surprisingly neat angle rules.

cards.text:
- **Inscribed angle**: an angle with its corner on the circle is **half** the **central angle** (corner at the centre) standing on the same arc.
- **Angle in a semicircle**: standing on a diameter, it's always **90°** (because the central angle is 180°).
- **Tangent**: a line touching the circle at one point is **at right angles to the radius** there.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 120"><circle cx="90" cy="60" r="50"/><circle class="dot" cx="90" cy="60" r="3"/><line class="faint" x1="50" y1="90" x2="90" y2="60"/><line class="faint" x1="130" y1="90" x2="90" y2="60"/><line class="a" x1="50" y1="90" x2="90" y2="10"/><line class="a" x1="130" y1="90" x2="90" y2="10"/><text x="80" y="80">2x</text><text x="84" y="32">x</text><text x="150" y="50">inscribed =</text><text x="150" y="66">½ central</text></svg>

cards.q: A central angle is 100°. What is the inscribed angle on the same arc?
An inscribed angle is 35°. What is the central angle on the same arc?
cards.explain: The central angle is twice the inscribed angle — 70°.

cards.q: A tangent touches a circle at P. The angle between the tangent and the radius to P is…

options.why: A tangent is always perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

options.feedback: It's always a right angle — 90°.

options.text: It depends on the circle's size
options.feedback: Any circle, any size — tangent and radius meet at 90°.

review.q: Any angle standing on a diameter, with its corner on the circle, measures…

options.feedback: 180° is the central angle on a diameter. The inscribed angle is half — 90°.
Always 90° — half of the 180° central angle.

congruence.title: Congruent shapes
congruence.summary: Exactly the same size and shape — one fits on the other after a slide, turn or flip.

cards.text: Two jigsaw pieces look identical. How could you prove they're exactly the same size and shape — without measuring every edge?
cards.reveal: Slide, turn or flip one until it sits **exactly on top** of the other. If it fits perfectly, they're **congruent**.

cards.text:
Two shapes are **congruent** (≅) if a rigid motion moves one exactly onto the other.

Then every matching side and matching angle is equal.

The order of letters matters: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A matches D, B matches E and C matches F.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 90"><polygon points="20,80 60,15 100,80"/><text x="10" y="88">A</text><text x="56" y="12">B</text><text x="100" y="88">C</text><polygon class="a" points="140,80 180,15 220,80"/><text x="130" y="88">D</text><text x="176" y="12">E</text><text x="220" y="88">F</text><text x="108" y="50">≅</text></svg>

cards.q: △ABC ≅ △DEF and AB = 5 cm. How long is DE?
cards.hint: A matches D and B matches E.
cards.explain: AB matches DE, and matching sides of congruent shapes are equal — 5 cm.

cards.q: △PQR ≅ △XYZ. Which angle equals ∠Q?

options.why: Q is the second letter, so it matches Y, the second letter.

options.feedback: X matches P (both first). Q is second, so it matches Y.
Z matches R (both third). Q matches Y.

review.q: Two shapes are congruent when…

options.text: A slide, turn or flip moves one exactly onto the other

options.feedback: Different shapes can share an area. Congruent means a rigid motion fits one exactly on the other.
Same angles but different sizes is similarity, not congruence.

coordinate_plane.title: The coordinate plane
coordinate_plane.summary: A grid where every point is a pair of numbers (x, y).

cards.text: How does a map app tell a delivery driver *exactly* where you are, using just two numbers?
cards.reveal: With **coordinates** — one number for across, one for up.

cards.text:
Two number lines cross at the **origin** (0, 0): the **x-axis** (across) and the **y-axis** (up).

A point is written **(x, y)**: go x across (right if positive), then y up (down if negative).

The axes split the plane into four **quadrants**, numbered I to IV anticlockwise from top right.

cards.q: In which quadrant is the point (−2, 5)?

options.why: Left (negative x) and up (positive y) is quadrant II.

options.feedback: Quadrant I needs both numbers positive. x = −2 is to the left.
Quadrant IV is right and down. (−2, 5) is left and up — quadrant II.

cards.q: How far apart are (1, 4) and (7, 4)?
cards.hint: They're at the same height, so just compare the x values.
cards.explain: Same y, so the distance is 7 − 1 = 6.

review.q: The point (0, 0) is called the…

options.feedback: The axes are the two number lines. Where they cross, (0, 0), is the origin.
Quadrants are the four regions. (0, 0) is the origin.

distance_formula.title: The distance formula
distance_formula.summary: Pythagoras on a grid: the straight-line distance between two points.

cards.text: A drone flies from (1, 2) to (4, 6) on a grid. How far did it fly in a straight line?
cards.reveal: **5 units** — and Pythagoras tells us how.

cards.text:
The straight line between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the **change in x** and the **change in y**.

**d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)**
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 110"><circle class="dot" cx="50" cy="95" r="4"/><circle class="dot" cx="140" cy="15" r="4"/><line class="a thick" x1="50" y1="95" x2="140" y2="15"/><line class="faint" x1="50" y1="95" x2="140" y2="95"/><line class="faint" x1="140" y1="95" x2="140" y2="15"/><text x="80" y="108">x₂ − x₁</text><text x="146" y="60">y₂ − y₁</text><text x="60" y="48">d</text></svg>

cards.title: Worked example
steps: Change in x = 4 − 1 = 3. Change in y = 6 − 2 = 4.

cards.q: How far is (0, 0) from (5, 12)?
How far is (−2, −1) from (4, 7)?

review.q: How far is (2, 3) from (5, 7)?

line_segment.title: Line segment
line_segment.summary: The straight piece of a line between two endpoints; its length is the distance between them.

cards.text: A line goes on forever. But the edge of your phone stops. So what is the edge of your phone?
cards.reveal: A **line segment** — the piece of a line between two endpoints.

cards.text:
A **line segment** AB is the part of a line from point A to point B, including both ends.

Its **length** is the distance from A to B. Its **midpoint** is the point exactly halfway.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 70"><line class="faint" x1="5" y1="35" x2="235" y2="35"/><line class="a thick" x1="50" y1="35" x2="190" y2="35"/><circle class="dot" cx="50" cy="35" r="4"/><circle class="dot" cx="190" cy="35" r="4"/><circle class="dot" cx="120" cy="35" r="3"/><text x="44" y="58">A</text><text x="184" y="58">B</text><text x="98" y="22">midpoint</text></svg>

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: On a number line, A is at 2 and B is at 9. How long is AB, and where is its midpoint?

cards.q: A is at −3 and B is at 5 on a number line. How long is segment AB?
cards.hint: Bigger minus smaller — careful with the minus sign.

cards.q: The midpoint of a segment from 4 to 10 is at…

review.q: A is at 1 and B is at 13. Where is the midpoint of AB?
How many endpoints does a line segment have?

options.feedback: One endpoint is a ray. A segment stops at both ends.
No endpoints is a full line. A segment has two.

parallel_lines.title: Parallel lines
parallel_lines.summary: Lines that never meet; a line crossing them makes matching equal angles.

cards.text: Railway tracks run side by side for hundreds of kilometres and never touch. What keeps them from crossing?
cards.reveal: They're **parallel** — they always point in the same direction, so they never meet.

cards.text:
**Parallel lines** lie in the same plane and never meet.

A **transversal** is a line that crosses them. It makes 8 angles, and they come in matching sets:

- **Corresponding** angles (same position at each crossing) are **equal**.
- **Alternate interior** angles (inside, opposite sides) are **equal**.
- **Co-interior** angles (inside, same side) **add to 180°**.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One angle is 65°. Find its corresponding angle and its co-interior partner.

cards.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One interior angle is 72°. What is its **co-interior** partner?
An alternate interior angle to a 50° angle is…

options.why: Alternate interior angles between parallel lines are equal.

options.feedback: 130° would be the co-interior partner (adds to 180°). Alternate angles are equal.
40° is the complement. Alternate interior angles are equal — 50°.

review.q: Between parallel lines, which angle pair **adds to 180°**?

options.feedback: Corresponding angles are equal, not supplementary.
Alternate interior angles are equal. Co-interior ones add to 180°.

polygon.title: Polygons
polygon.summary: A closed flat shape with straight sides; its inside angles add to (n − 2) × 180°.

cards.text: A stop sign has 8 sides. Without measuring, can you say what all its inside angles add up to?
cards.reveal: Yes — **1080°**. Every polygon follows the same simple rule. Let's find it.

cards.text:
A **polygon** is a closed flat shape made only of straight line segments (its **sides**), meeting at **vertices**.

Triangle (3 sides), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6), octagon (8)…

A circle is **not** a polygon — it has no straight sides.

cards.title: The angle-sum rule
cards.problem: Why do a polygon's inside angles add to (n − 2) × 180°?
steps: From one corner, draw lines to every other corner. A polygon with **n** sides splits into **n − 2** triangles.

cards.q: What do the inside angles of a **hexagon** (6 sides) add up to?
A regular octagon has 8 equal angles. How big is each one?
cards.hint: Find the total first, then share it equally.

review.q: What do the inside angles of a pentagon add up to?
Which of these is **not** a polygon?

options.feedback: A triangle is made of 3 straight sides — a polygon.
A stop sign is an octagon — 8 straight sides.

pythagorean_theorem.title: Pythagoras' theorem
pythagorean_theorem.summary: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c² — the two short sides' squares add up to the longest side's square.

cards.text: Builders mark 3 m along one wall, 4 m along the other, and check the diagonal is exactly 5 m. Why does that guarantee a perfect square corner?
cards.reveal: Because 3² + 4² = 5². That's **Pythagoras' theorem** — and it works in reverse too.

cards.text:
In a **right triangle**, the longest side (opposite the right angle) is the **hypotenuse**, c. The other two are the legs, a and b.

**a² + b² = c²**

The squares on the two legs together have exactly the area of the square on the hypotenuse.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 110"><polygon points="40,90 40,30 120,90"/><rect class="a" x="40" y="82" width="8" height="8"/><text x="24" y="64">a</text><text x="76" y="104">b</text><text x="86" y="54">c</text><text x="140" y="60">a² + b² = c²</text></svg>

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: A right triangle has legs 3 and 4. How long is the hypotenuse?

cards.q: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
The hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5. How long is the other leg?
Do sides 7, 24 and 25 make a right triangle?

options.why: 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². When the squares add up, the corner is square.

options.feedback: Many sets work. Check — 49 + 576 = 625 = 25².

review.q: A 10 m ladder leans on a wall with its foot 6 m out. How high up the wall does it reach?
The hypotenuse is always…

options.text: The side opposite the right angle (the longest)

options.feedback: The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.

options.text: Any side next to the right angle
options.feedback: Those are the legs. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.

quadrilateral.title: Four-sided shapes
quadrilateral.summary: A four-sided shape — parallelograms, rectangles, rhombi, squares and more; angles add to 360°.

cards.text: Is a square a rectangle? Is a rectangle a square? People argue about this — the answer is surprisingly neat.
cards.reveal: Every square **is** a rectangle (four right angles), but not every rectangle is a square.

cards.text:
A **quadrilateral** has 4 sides; its angles add to **360°** (two triangles).

- **Parallelogram** — both pairs of opposite sides parallel (and equal).
- **Rectangle** — a parallelogram with four right angles.
- **Rhombus** — a parallelogram with four equal sides.
- **Square** — both a rectangle and a rhombus.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 70"><polygon points="10,60 30,15 90,15 70,60"/><text x="14" y="70">parallelogram</text><rect class="a" x="110" y="15" width="55" height="45"/><text x="112" y="70">rectangle</text><rect x="185" y="15" width="45" height="45"/><text x="190" y="70">square</text></svg>

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95° and 100°. Find the fourth.

cards.q: In a parallelogram, one angle is 70°. What is the angle **next to it**?
cards.hint: Neighbouring angles sit between parallel sides, like co-interior angles.
cards.explain: Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add to 180°, so 180° − 70° = 110°.

cards.q: Is every square a rhombus?

options.text: Yes — it has four equal sides
options.why: A rhombus only needs four equal sides; a square has them (plus right angles).

options.text: No — a rhombus has no right angles
options.feedback: A rhombus may have right angles; it just doesn't need them. A square is a special rhombus.

review.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, 90° and 110°. What is the fourth?

ray.title: Ray
ray.summary: A straight path that starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction.

cards.text: A torch beam starts at the bulb and goes on and on. Is it a line, a segment, or something else?
cards.reveal: Something in between — a **ray**. It has a start but no end.

cards.text:
A **ray** starts at one endpoint and goes forever in one direction.

Ray **AB** starts at A and passes through B. The endpoint is always named first, so ray AB and ray BA point opposite ways.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 70"><line class="a thick" x1="40" y1="35" x2="225" y2="35"/><polyline class="a" points="215,28 227,35 215,42"/><circle class="dot" cx="40" cy="35" r="4"/><circle class="dot" cx="130" cy="35" r="4"/><text x="34" y="58">A</text><text x="125" y="58">B</text><text x="150" y="22">ray AB →</text></svg>

cards.q: Are ray AB and ray BA the same ray?

options.text: No — they start at different points and point opposite ways
options.why: Right. Ray AB starts at A; ray BA starts at B and heads back through A.

options.text: Yes — they use the same two points
options.feedback: The order matters. The first letter is where the ray starts.

cards.q: Which of these is best described as a ray?

options.text: A laser beam from a pointer
options.why: It starts at the pointer and keeps going in one direction.

options.feedback: A table edge has two ends — that's a segment.

options.text: A road that goes on forever both ways
options.feedback: Endless both ways is a line. A ray has exactly one end.

review.q: Ray PQ starts at…

options.feedback: The first letter names the endpoint — ray PQ starts at P.
A ray starts at its endpoint, the first letter — P.

rigid_motion.title: Slides, turns and flips
rigid_motion.summary: Sliding, turning or flipping a shape without changing its size or shape.

cards.text: In a video game, a character slides across the screen, spins around and faces the other way — but never gets bigger or squashed. What kind of moves are these?
cards.reveal: **Rigid motions** — moves that keep every length and angle exactly the same.

cards.text:
A **rigid motion** moves a shape without changing its size or shape. There are three basic kinds:

- **Translation** — slide it.
- **Rotation** — turn it around a point.
- **Reflection** — flip it over a line, like a mirror.

After any rigid motion, every distance and every angle stays the same.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 80"><polygon points="10,60 30,20 45,60"/><polygon class="a" points="50,60 70,20 85,60"/><text x="18" y="76">slide</text><polygon points="115,65 130,30 145,65"/><polygon class="a" points="165,45 130,30 165,15"/><circle class="dot" cx="130" cy="30" r="2.5"/><text x="118" y="78">turn</text><line class="faint" x1="205" y1="10" x2="205" y2="70"/><polygon points="172,60 190,20 198,60"/><polygon class="a" points="238,60 220,20 212,60"/><text x="192" y="78">flip</text></svg>

cards.q: You rotate a 4 cm line segment by 90°. How long is it afterwards?
cards.reveal: Still **4 cm**. Rotations, like all rigid motions, never change lengths.

cards.q: Which of these is **not** a rigid motion?

options.text: Stretching a photo to make it wider
options.why: Stretching changes lengths, so it isn't rigid.

options.text: Sliding a book across a table
options.feedback: A slide (translation) keeps size and shape — it's rigid.

options.text: Seeing your face in a mirror
options.feedback: A mirror image is a reflection — rigid. Stretching is the one that isn't.

cards.q: A shape is flipped over a line. Its angles…

options.why: Reflections keep every angle and length.

options.feedback: A flip doesn't resize anything — angles stay the same.
Nothing changes size in a reflection; each angle keeps its measure.

review.q: Turning a shape around a fixed point is called a…

options.feedback: A translation slides without turning.
A reflection flips over a line. Turning is rotation.

similarity.title: Similar shapes
similarity.summary: Same shape, different size: equal angles and sides in the same ratio.

cards.text: When you zoom into a photo, everything gets bigger — but faces don't look stretched. What stays the same?
cards.reveal: The **angles** and the **proportions**. The zoomed photo is **similar** to the original.

cards.text:
Two shapes are **similar** (∼) if one is a scaled copy of the other (possibly also slid, turned or flipped).

- Matching **angles are equal**.
- Matching **sides are in the same ratio**, the **scale factor** k.

Scale factor 2 doubles every length; ½ halves it.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: Triangle sides 3, 4, 5 are scaled by a factor of 2. Find the new sides.
steps: **6, 8 and 10**. The angles don't change at all.

cards.q: A shape is scaled by a factor of 3. A side that was 4 cm becomes…
Two similar triangles have matching sides 4 and 6. Another side of the small triangle is 6. How long is the matching side of the big one?
cards.hint: Find the scale factor first (big ÷ small).

review.q: In similar shapes, matching angles are…

options.feedback: Scaling changes lengths, never angles.
Matching angles of similar shapes are equal.

review.q: A model car is built at scale ½. Its real wheel is 60 cm across. How wide is the model's wheel?
review.explain: Scale ½ halves every length — 60 ÷ 2 = 30 cm.

triangle.title: Triangles
triangle.summary: A three-sided shape whose angles always add up to 180°.

cards.text: Tear the three corners off any paper triangle and put them side by side. What shape do they always make?
cards.reveal: A **straight line**. That's why every triangle's angles add up to **180°**.

cards.text:
A **triangle** is a polygon with 3 sides. Its three inside angles always add up to **180°**.

By sides, a triangle is **equilateral** (all 3 equal), **isosceles** (2 equal) or **scalene** (none equal).

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. Find the third.

cards.q: A right triangle has one angle of 35°. What is the third angle?
cards.hint: A right triangle already has one 90° angle.

cards.q: Each angle of an **equilateral** triangle measures…

review.q: Two angles of a triangle are 40° and 75°. What is the third?
A triangle with exactly two equal sides is…

options.feedback: Equilateral means all three sides are equal.
Scalene means no sides are equal.

triangle_congruence_criteria.title: Proving triangles match
triangle_congruence_criteria.summary: SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS — three matching parts that prove two triangles are identical.

cards.text: A triangle has 6 parts — 3 sides and 3 angles. To prove two triangles are congruent, do you really need to check all 6?
cards.reveal: No — just **3 well-chosen parts** are enough. Which three is the clever bit.

cards.text:
Two triangles are congruent if they match in any of these:

- **SSS** — all three sides.
- **SAS** — two sides and the angle **between** them.
- **ASA** — two angles and the side **between** them.
- **AAS** — two angles and a side **not** between them.

**AAA does not work**: same angles can still be different sizes.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 80"><polygon points="10,70 50,15 100,70"/><line class="a thick" x1="10" y1="70" x2="50" y2="15"/><line class="a thick" x1="10" y1="70" x2="100" y2="70"/><path class="a" d="M28,70 A18,18 0 0 0 21,55"/><text x="38" y="64">A</text><text x="2" y="38">S</text><text x="50" y="80">S</text><text x="120" y="45">SAS: angle between</text><text x="120" y="62">the two sides</text></svg>

cards.q: Two triangles have two equal sides and the **angle between them** is equal. Which rule proves they're congruent?

options.feedback: SSS needs all three sides. Here we know two sides and the angle between.
AAA never proves congruence. This is SAS.

cards.q: Which of these does **not** prove two triangles are congruent?

options.why: A small and a large equilateral triangle have the same angles but different sizes.

options.feedback: SSS always proves congruence. AAA is the one that fails.

options.text: Two angles and the side between them (ASA)
options.feedback: ASA always proves congruence. AAA is the one that fails.

cards.q: Put the steps of a congruence proof in order:
items: Mark the equal parts you know
Check they match a rule (SSS, SAS, ASA or AAS)
Use it — matching parts are equal
cards.explain: Evidence, then the rule, then the conclusion — and only then use the matching parts.

review.q: Two angles and the side **between** them match. That's…

options.feedback: AAS is when the side is not between the two angles.
SAS is two sides with the angle between them.

triangle_similarity_criteria.title: Spotting similar triangles
triangle_similarity_criteria.summary: AA, SAS∼ and SSS∼ — quick tests that two triangles are similar.

cards.text: How could you measure a tree's height with only a measuring tape and a sunny day?
cards.reveal: Measure **shadows**. The tree and a stick make **similar triangles** with their shadows.

cards.text:
Two triangles are similar if:

- **AA** — two angles match (the third then matches too), or
- **SAS∼** — two pairs of sides are in the same ratio with the angle between them equal, or
- **SSS∼** — all three pairs of sides are in the same ratio.

AA is the one you'll use most.

cards.title: Worked example — the tree
cards.problem: A 2 m stick casts a 3 m shadow. At the same moment a tree casts a 15 m shadow. How tall is the tree?
steps: The sun hits both at the same angle, and both stand at right angles to the ground → **AA**, so the triangles are similar.

cards.q: A 1.5 m person casts a 2 m shadow. A building casts a 40 m shadow. How tall is the building?
Two triangles each have angles of 40° and 60°. Are they similar?

options.why: Two matching angles are enough; the third must be 80° in both.

options.text: Only if their sides are equal
options.feedback: Equal sides would make them congruent. For similarity, two equal angles (AA) is enough.

options.text: We can't tell without the sides
options.feedback: Angles alone are enough for similarity — that's the AA rule.

review.q: The quickest test for similar triangles is…

options.feedback: One side tells you very little. Two matching angles (AA) prove similarity.
Similar triangles usually have different areas. Use AA.

trigonometric_ratios.title: Sin, cos and tan
trigonometric_ratios.summary: sin, cos and tan — side ratios in a right triangle that depend only on the angle.

cards.text: A surveyor can find the height of a mountain without climbing it — just by measuring one angle and one distance. How?
cards.reveal: With **trigonometric ratios**. In similar right triangles, the side ratios depend only on the angle.

cards.text:
In a right triangle, pick an angle θ. Name the sides from θ's point of view: **opposite**, **adjacent** (next to it, not the hypotenuse) and **hypotenuse**.

- **sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse**
- **cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse**
- **tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent**

Memory trick: **SOH CAH TOA**.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 240 110"><polygon points="30,95 190,95 190,20"/><rect class="a" x="182" y="87" width="8" height="8"/><path class="a" d="M60,95 A30,30 0 0 0 57,82"/><text x="64" y="90">θ</text><text x="196" y="62">opposite</text><text x="88" y="108">adjacent</text><text x="80" y="50">hypotenuse</text></svg>

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: A right triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. For the angle θ opposite the side 3, find sin, cos and tan.

cards.q: In a right triangle the side adjacent to θ is 8 and the hypotenuse is 10. What is cos θ?
A 12 m ramp rises at 30° to the ground. How high does it rise? (sin 30° = 0.5)
cards.hint: Height is opposite the 30° angle; the ramp is the hypotenuse.

cards.q: A 10 m ladder makes a 60° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? (Round to 2 decimal places.)
cards.hint: Use sin, and a calculator for sin 60°.

review.q: Which ratio is opposite ÷ adjacent?

options.feedback: sin is opposite ÷ hypotenuse (SOH).
cos is adjacent ÷ hypotenuse (CAH).

review.q: The side opposite θ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 10. What is sin θ?
